title: A Hebrew - English Bible According to the Masoretic Text and the JPS 1917 Edition
notes: Public-domain 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation. Cited for quotations: Genesis 2:2, 12:1, 17:5, 17:7, 17:10-12; Exodus 20 (opening words and the Sabbath commandment); Exodus 23:19, 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21 (kid in its mother's milk); Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:4; Psalm 137:1.

title: Abraham
notes: Cited for: Abraham left Ur in Mesopotamia for a land he later learned was Canaan; best known for the depth of his faith; Islam traces Muhammad to Ishmael; Christianity traces Jesus' genealogy to Isaac.

title: Covenant (religion)
notes: Cited for: covenant (berit) as a binding agreement; God bound himself by oath to fulfill promises to Abraham.

title: Judaism: Biblical Judaism (20th-4th century BCE)
notes: Cited for: Abraham promised the land of Canaan and numerous progeny; at Sinai God made the Israelites his people and gave the terms of his covenant; the historicity of an escape from Egypt by some component of the later Israelite tribes.

title: Judaism: Basic practices and institutions
notes: Cited for: circumcision on the eighth day as a covenantal sign (berit mila), with benedictions and naming.

title: Circumcision
notes: Cited for: in Judaism circumcision represents the fulfillment of the covenant between God and Abraham (Genesis 17).

title: Moses
notes: Cited for: the biblical account of enslavement, plagues and the Red Sea crossing; the covenant ceremony at Sinai and the Ten Commandments; Moses revered in Judaism as the greatest prophet and teacher.

title: Were the Jews Slaves in Egypt? (S. David Sperling)
notes: Cited for: Bible scholar S. David Sperling (Hebrew Union College) notes there is no archaeological evidence that the Israelites were ever in Egypt. Attributed to the named scholar.

title: Israel (biblical kingdom)
notes: Cited for: the earliest widely accepted mention of the name Israel is an inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah from about 1205 BCE.

title: Torah
notes: Cited for: the oral Torah, laws and customs passed down orally, held by many Jews to be part of God's revelation to Moses; Torah scrolls removed and returned with special reverence.

title: Hebrew Bible: Books of the Hebrew Bible
notes: Cited for: Tanakh as an acronym of Torah (Instruction or Law), Neviim (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings); the Torah's five books; 24 books, one per ancient scroll; Christians divided some books into parts.

title: Sefer Torah
notes: Cited for: the Torah scroll written in Hebrew by a qualified scribe (sofer) on parchment, kept in the ark; read on Sabbaths, Mondays, Thursdays and festivals.

title: Simchat Torah
notes: Cited for: the yearly Torah reading cycle ends with Deuteronomy and restarts with Genesis on Simchat Torah; seven circles (haqafot) around the bimah with the scrolls, dancing.

title: Temple of Jerusalem
notes: Cited for: First Temple completed under Solomon in 957 BCE and made the only place of sacrifice in Judah; Second Temple completed 515 BCE; destroyed by Rome in 70 CE during the Jewish rebellion.

title: Babylonian Exile
notes: Cited for: destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 BCE and deportation to Babylonia; exiles kept the Sabbath and holidays, circumcision, prayers in place of sacrifices; synagogues may have begun then; Cyrus allowed return in 538 BCE; some stayed.

title: Western Wall
notes: Cited for: the Western Wall as the only remains of the Temple Mount's retaining wall; a place of prayer and pilgrimage; slips of paper with prayers pushed into its cracks.

title: Tisha b'Av
notes: Cited for: Tisha b'Av (9 Av, July or August) as a day of mourning and fasting for the destruction of the First and Second Temples; reading of Lamentations.

title: Johanan ben Zakkai
notes: Cited for: disciples credited with smuggling him out of Jerusalem in a coffin; academy at Jamnia (Jabneh); Temple ceremonies kept elsewhere "to serve as memorials of the Sanctuary"; fixed the conditions for Judaism after the Temple.

title: Synagogue
notes: Cited for: house of prayer, assembly and study; after 70 CE the focal point of Jewish religious life; a liturgy with no sacrifice needs no priesthood.

title: Minyan
notes: Cited for: a quorum of ten for communal prayer, traditionally men; without it no public Torah reading; Reform and Conservative Judaism allow women to complete a minyan.

title: Diaspora (Judaism)
notes: Cited for: the Diaspora as Jewish communities scattered outside the land; Jewish life centered on synagogues, Torah study and prayer.

title: Rabbi
notes: Cited for: rabbi means "my teacher" or "my master"; by 100 CE the term denoted a sage, an interpreter of Jewish law.

title: Mishna
notes: Cited for: the Mishnah as the oldest authoritative postbiblical collection and codification of Jewish oral laws, given final form early in the 3rd century CE by Judah ha-Nasi; Mishnah and Gemara make up the Talmud.

title: Talmud and Midrash
notes: Cited for: the Talmud as Mishnah plus Gemara; its sages debating each text to exhaust its meaning.

title: Babylonian Talmud
notes: Cited for: completed about 600 CE; the more authoritative of the two Talmuds; the constitution and bylaws of Rabbinic Judaism.

title: Sabbath (Judaism)
notes: Cited for: sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday; the only Jewish holiday in the Ten Commandments; 39 categories of forbidden work, suspended when life or health is in danger; candles, Kiddush, two challah loaves; varied observance across branches.

title: Challah
notes: Cited for: two loaves of challah on Friday evening commemorating the double portion of manna.

title: Havdala
notes: Cited for: havdalah blessings over wine, spices and a braided candle, distinguishing holy from ordinary at the Sabbath's end.

title: Heschel's Vision of the Sabbath: A Contemporary Challenge (Or Rose)
notes: Cited for: Abraham Joshua Heschel's 1951 book The Sabbath calls the Sabbath "a palace in time" and places holiness in time rather than in space.

title: What is Rosh Hashanah, and when is it observed?
notes: Cited for: Rosh Hashanah on 1 Tishri (September or October) opens the Ten Days of Repentance, which end on Yom Kippur.

title: Shofar
notes: Cited for: the shofar, a ram's horn, sounded on Rosh Hashanah to call people to spiritual reawakening.

title: Yom Kippur
notes: Cited for: the holiest and most solemn Jewish holiday; a 25-hour fast; forgiveness asked of friends beforehand, since forgiveness from one's fellows signifies God's forgiveness.

title: Sukkot
notes: Cited for: begins five days after Yom Kippur; huts roofed with branches or thatch; meals and sometimes sleep in them; recalls the 40 years in the wilderness.

title: Passover
notes: Cited for: Passover (March or April) commemorates liberation from slavery in Egypt; the seder and the Haggadah; matzo because the dough had not leavened; children's four questions.

title: Hanukkah
notes: Cited for: Hanukkah means "dedication"; the Maccabees' rededication of the Second Temple in 164 BCE; one more candle each night for eight days; the Talmud's oil story; traditionally a minor holiday not in the Hebrew Scriptures.

title: Mitzvah
notes: Cited for: a mitzvah is any commandment in the Torah; the Talmud counts 613 (248 mandatory, 365 prohibitive); rabbinic additions such as lighting festival candles; good deeds as fulfilling mitzvahs.

title: Kashruth
notes: Cited for: kosher means "fit" or "proper"; permitted fish, birds and mammals; strict separation of meat and dairy with distinct dishes; ritual slaughter and salting; for observant Jews no motive beyond God's command is needed.

title: Jewish practices and customs (Jewish Americans in 2020)
notes: Survey fielded Nov. 2019 to June 2020. Cited for: 17% of US Jews keep kosher at home; 95% of Orthodox, 24% of Conservative and 5% of Reform Jews.

title: Jewish Americans in 2020
notes: Survey fielded Nov. 2019 to June 2020. Cited for: 37% of US Jews identify as Reform, 17% Conservative, 9% Orthodox, about 4% other branches, 32% no particular branch.

title: Orthodox Judaism
notes: Cited for: Written and Oral Law immutably fixed and the sole norm of observance; daily worship, kashruth, Torah study, separate seating.

title: Reform Judaism
notes: Cited for: began early in the 19th century in Germany with lay appeals to update worship; first Reform services in 1810 with organ, choir and German prayers; Judaism as a living, developing faith; questions the binding force of ritual law.

title: Conservative Judaism
notes: Cited for: inspired by Zacharias Frankel; the Law sacred as a living force; modernization less radical than Reform; ordaining women rabbis from 1985.

title: Ashkenazi
notes: Cited for: Jews of the Rhineland and France who moved east to Poland, Lithuania and Russia, and their descendants; widespread use of Yiddish.

title: Sephardi
notes: Cited for: descendants of the Jews of Spain and Portugal; Judeo-Spanish (Ladino); differences from Ashkenazim are of traditional expression, not sect; Mizrahim as the more proper term for Jews of North Africa and the Middle East.
